touches.text: Every verb anywhere is reached from the cairn command, as a path: cairn <device> [<machine> ...] <verb>. No central list: help at any level prints that level's own verbs under [<name>], alpha order, then calls back up the tree to its parent, which does the same, out to [cairn]. The groups come out flat, one after another, not nested: cairn codemother inspector_gadget help  -> [inspector_gadget] ... then [codemother] ... then [cairn] ... A device may ask another device help over the bus the same way; nothing being built needs that yet. (Q#2, Akien 2026-11-03)

The launcher walks the words. `cairn cairn foo bar` (the long form) means "tell the cairn device to run foo with argument bar". At each level: is the next word a machine here? Step into it and take the next word. Is it a script in this level's bin/? Run it, pass back the result, done. Neither? It is a bus verb: send it to this level over the bus. So `cairn foo bar baz`: foo is a device; it has a machine bar; bar's bin/ has baz, so baz runs. No bar machine? bar goes to foo over the bus. Each check is one directory lookup, so it is fast. (Q#12, Akien 2026-11-03)

Two execution trees: at each segment, if there is a script for it in that device's bin, run it; otherwise go onto the bus and ask that device. Why: scripts are the simple path, and the bus is the operator's route to what a device answers itself, often faster (eg `cairn codemother show artifact <id>`). (Akien, 2026-11-05)
bus_client: gets a process onto the bus (reach a device, or connect).
